Fantasy story excerpt:
Every tree in the valley could remember the future. Beneath the oldest oak, the traveler asked
512.completion:
:
‘Long lost one, strange and dark, guide me and lead me. Whisper the words so I might enter your realm.’
No one understood his words, but the trees sighed sadly and began to whisper. Ever since the event known as “The Apocalypse”, the trees held the knowledge. It was written in the wind and the traveler sat with his legs crossed. The wind shook him and he felt it deeply. Its message was clear and made him look at himself. Was he really the right one? He did not think so, but it was right time. He looked at the thousands of little flowers around him. They seemed to hum their songs to the tune made by the breeze. The wind went to the other side of the hill, to the other valley, then back again. It shook the grass and it really seemed that the entire world was meant to speak to the traveler. He could barely hear the whisper, but it was loud enough.
He had no choice. The time was right and the apocalypse came, again. Slowly darkness fell over the grass as the clouds turned dark and the thunder began. He had to destroy the world to save it, yet again.
He stood up, and faced the valley. No one called for his attention. It was only him and the Apocalypse. He took out his golden sword. He was as shiny in the dark, cold rain.
‘Help me’, he whispered.

(From the novel The World Eater by Lyrik Lyons)

512.prompt:
Fantasy story excerpt:
The moon was made of glass. Each winter, the royal mason climbed a silver ladder to repair its cracks. Tonight, he
512.completion:
was mending a crescent-shaped shatter near the top—a pale gash that glowed brightly in the dark sky, almost like a crack in a window. Together, he and the moon looked like a contest between light and dark: he, a silhouette; the moon, a burst of silver. The repairs would take all night.

The sounds of spring were muted beneath my bedroom window—the cheerful chirping of birds, the whistle of the wind through branches, and all the restless whisper of leaves.

I missed that whispering already. “I do not mind the quiet of the snow,” I told the moon. “It means you are happy.”

“I love the snow, Papa,” I said. “December is my favourite month. Even though I know that you hate it.”

I sighed. The moon sighed too.

“Soon, it will be summer,” I said. The moon listened.

“When it’s summer, you’ll be back to riding your motorcycle and exploring strange new places. You love those cycles.”

“But I like the quiet in winter,” I said. “I like the cold, too.”

The moon sighed once more. I pulled my grandmother’s patchwork quilt tighter around me as the night air grew colder.

“I hope you discover America and France,” I said, “and many other places.”

The moon glowed brighter.

“Come back soon,” I said. “Very soon. I need you. I love you. I don’t want you to go.”

The moon sighed again, then dimmed to twilight. I watched the silhouette of the mason disappear from its edges, and the shadows of the shutters on my windows closed with a click.

Author Bio:
Mark has been telling stories his whole life. He has composed tales for professional use, and more often, just for fun. He enjoys using his imagination because it means he can escape through the written word. He has always been of the opinion that he is only limited by his imagination.<start_of_image>By his late twenties, he was hired as a writer for a publishing company. He came into contact with editors, but it quickly became a game of fighting his ideas against what the company wanted. So, in the early three thousands, he put aside his stories and his aspirations and went to work for a computer development company. For a time, his computer skills, his writing skills, and his marketing skills were happily in league. For nearly two decades, he designed websites, wrote articles, and managed social media accounts. He has lived in Virginia, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and now calls North Carolina his home. When he’s not working, he likes to hang out at his local coffee shop.

Mark currently has a novel waiting for a publisher, and he hopes they are just as anxious to read his story as he is to share it with them. The novel is an urban fantasy set in modern day, but the main character is a ghost of over two hundred years.

Janet Kenny
